subject: MARCUSE et al. (1953)
object: MARCUSE et al. (1953) reported 2 cases of hamartoma of the hypothalamus with associated developmental defects.

subject: Encha-Razavi et al. (1992)
object: Encha-Razavi et al. (1992) reported congenital hypothalamic hamartomas found at autopsy in 3 unrelated fetuses. In 2 of the fetuses the tumor was associated only with skeletal dysplasia. In the third it was part of a nonrandom association of congenital malformations suggestive of Meckel syndrome.

subject: Encha-Razavi et al. (1992)
object: Encha-Razavi et al. (1992) noted that in one family, a previous boy had died soon after birth with similar craniofacial and skeletal abnormalities. They suggested the disorder may be familial.

subject: Encha-Razavi et al. (1992)
object: Encha-Razavi et al. (1992) reviewed reported cases of Pallister-Hall syndrome and found that only skeletal dysplasia and orofacial abnormalities were consistently present, resembling the findings in their first 2 cases. They proposed these features as the minimum criteria for a distinct, possibly familial entity, which they suggested calling 'congenital hypothalamic hamartoma syndrome' (CHHS).

subject: Craig et al. (2008)
object: Craig et al. (2008) studied 55 patients with sporadic, nonsyndromic hypothalamic hamartoma and intractable epilepsy, comparing genomic DNA from peripheral blood with DNA from surgically resected HH tissue. Resequencing of GLI3 found no causative germline mutations.

subject: Craig et al. (2008)
object: Craig et al. (2008) found somatic (tumor-only) chromosomal abnormalities involving the GLI3 locus in 8 of 55 (15%) resected hypothalamic hamartoma tissue samples. Copy-number analysis on Affymetrix 10K SNP arrays identified a somatic abnormality on chromosome 7p in one sample. GLI3 resequencing showed loss of heterozygosity (LOH) within GLI3 in 3 samples, and genotyping of 28 SNPs in and around GLI3 found LOH in 5 more. The authors concluded that these somatic GLI3 abnormalities are associated with HH pathogenesis in sporadic, nonsyndromic patients, and noted that the abnormalities appeared highly variable.

subject: Craig et al. (2008)
object: Craig et al. (2008) described hypothalamic hamartomas as rare, benign congenital tumors associated with intractable epilepsy. Most cases are sporadic and nonsyndromic, and about 5% are associated with Pallister-Hall syndrome, which is caused by haploinsufficiency of GLI3.

subject: Rubino et al. (2019)
object: Rubino et al. (2019) described 2 brothers with a familial syndrome of hypothalamic hamartomas and polydactyly that differed from Pallister-Hall syndrome. One brother had a large hypothalamic hamartoma that was biopsied and subtotally resected by an endoscopic endonasal approach, and the authors reported its histopathologic findings.

subject: Rubino et al. (2019)
object: Rubino et al. (2019) attributed the familial syndrome of hypothalamic hamartomas and polydactyly in 2 brothers to germline mutations in the SMO gene. They stated that this was the first familial syndrome reported to be caused by germline SMO mutations, and the first familial syndrome other than Pallister-Hall syndrome to be associated with hypothalamic hamartomas.

subject: Rubino et al. (2019)
object: Rubino et al. (2019) contrasted the syndrome in their family, which they attributed to germline SMO mutations, with Pallister-Hall syndrome. They noted that Pallister-Hall syndrome is autosomal dominant and is caused by truncation of GLI3, a downstream effector in the sonic hedgehog pathway.

subject: Le et al. (2020)
object: Le et al. (2020) reported 7 individuals from 5 independent families with a wide spectrum of developmental anomalies. These affected the brain (hypothalamic hamartoma and microcephaly), the heart (atrioventricular septal defect), the skeleton (postaxial polydactyly, narrow chest, and shortening of long bones), and the enteric nervous system (aganglionosis).

subject: Le et al. (2020)
object: In 7 affected individuals from 5 independent families with developmental anomalies, Le et al. (2020) identified biallelic loss-of-function variants in the SMO gene. The abstract does not list the individual variants.

subject: Le et al. (2020)
object: Le et al. (2020) found that cells from affected individuals had normal ciliogenesis but severely altered hedgehog signal transduction. This resulted either from altered trafficking at the primary cilium or from abnormal activation of the pathway downstream of SMO. GLI2 accumulated at the ciliary tip independently of hedgehog stimulation, which the authors suggested points to a role for SMO in regulating basal ciliary trafficking of GLI2 when the pathway is off.
